q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 aim to retrieve the distinct (ITM.ITEMN, VENDN) pairs for ITM records with ITEMN between 1 and 20 that have at least one associated ITP record (linked via ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN) and a corresponding PUR record (linked via ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM) having PUR.ODATE > 85. Q1 achieves this by first creating a subquery (with DISTINCT) from ITP join PUR and then joining that with ITM, while Q2 directly joins ITM, ITP, and PUR and uses DISTINCT on the overall result. Since the join conditions and filtering are essentially the same and ITM.ITEMN is the primary key, the queries are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Both queries join R1 and two copies of R2 imposing the same equality on the A column. Since R2’s primary key is A, any two rows with the same A must have the same B value, making the additional condition Y.B = Z.B in Q1 redundant. As a result, both queries yield the same result set.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Both queries achieve the same objective: they filter the ITP table for rows with NP > 1000 and join those rows with ITM on matching ITEMNO. Q1 performs a subquery that selects distinct (ITEMNO, NP) pairs before joining, while Q2 applies DISTINCT on the final join result. Since ITM.ITEMNO is a primary key (guaranteeing one row per ITEMNO) and any duplicate rows in ITP are removed by the final DISTINCT in Q2, the two queries return the same set of rows.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Both queries are intended to produce the same final result: pairs of ITM.ITEMNO and NP from ITP where the ITEMNO values match. Q1 first removes duplicates from ITP (based on ITEMNO and NP) in a subquery and then joins with ITM, while Q2 performs the join between ITP and ITM and removes any duplicates in the final output with DISTINCT. Because ITM.ITEMNO is unique (the primary key) and the DISTINCT in Q2 will eliminate duplicate rows that might arise from multiple identical rows in ITP, the semantics of the two queries are equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Both queries ultimately return the same set of ITP rows whose ITEMN appears in an ITL row with WKCEN=468 and LOCAN=0. Q1 uses an IN subquery, while Q2 performs an inner join (with duplicates removed by DISTINCT). Thus, they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 simply finds all team members from teams whose project matches the project of a department named 'SECURITY'. Q2, however, only returns a team member if there is a payroll record that links that employee to a department by having the department name in the PDEPT field. Thus, if an employee appears in TEAMS and the department 'SECURITY' but his payroll record has a PDEPT different from 'SECURITY', Q1 returns him while Q2 does not.
counterexample_dsp: A department 'SECURITY' is defined with a project 1. A team record joins that project with an employee (say, 10). However, the payroll record for employee 10 has a PDEPT that is not 'SECURITY' (for example, 'FINANCE'). In this case Q1 returns employee 10 while Q2 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Both queries aim to retrieve applicants for which there is a payroll entry with DEPTNO = 29. However, Q1 does the join by verifying that the payroll row used in the join itself has DEPTNO = 29, whereas Q2 joins APPLICANT to an arbitrary payroll record A (with no filtering on DEPTNO) and separately joins a derived payroll table B that is filtered by DEPTNO = 29. In cases where an applicant’s SSNO appears in payroll more than once (one row with DEPTNO = 29 and another with a different DEPTNO), Q1 returns one join from the matching DEPTNO = 29 row, but Q2 will combine the non-filtered payroll row A with the DEPTNO = 29 row in B, causing duplicate output rows. Hence, they are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: In PAYROLL, include two rows for the same SSNO: one with DEPTNO = 29 and one with another DEPTNO (e.g. 30). In APPLICANT, include a record with that SSNO. Q1 returns one result (because only the row with DEPTNO = 29 qualifies), while Q2 returns duplicate rows because both payroll rows for that SSNO can join with the derived row from PAYROLL where DEPTNO = 29.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Both queries aim to return employees whose (EMP, DEPT) pair matches a (MGR, DEPT) in DEPT where LOC = 3. However, Q1 uses a tuple IN predicate so that each employee is returned once, while Q2 explicitly joins EMP and DEPT and will return one output row for every matching DEPT row (thus it may return duplicates).
counterexample_dsp: Create one employee and two duplicate DEPT rows (both with LOC = 3 and the same (MGR, DEPT)) that match the employee. Q1 returns a single row but Q2 returns two rows.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Q1 returns only rows where A is exactly 5 and C is less than 1, while Q2 returns rows where A is less than 10. This means Q2 will include records (e.g., with A=7) that Q1 does not.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (7, 10, 2);
counterexample_dsp: A row with A=7 (e.g., (7, 10, 2)) satisfies Q2 (7 < 10) but not Q1 (7 != 5).

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 returns all users from USER with CITY = 3 and displays a count of pictures with SIZE > 1000000 (using 0 if none exist), while Q2 only returns users that have at least one matching picture because it uses an inner join. Thus, a city=3 user without any large pictures will appear in Q1 (with count 0) but be absent from Q2.
counterexample_dsp: A test case with a user in city 3 who has no pictures.large enough (i.e., no picture with SIZE > 1000000). Q1 would output that user with count 0, but Q2 would not output any row for that user.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: Both queries aim to return users that have at least one PIC record with PICSIZE < 500000 (alias U) and at least one PIC record with PICSIZE >= 500000 (alias V). In Q1 an additional join to PIC (alias W) is added with the condition that W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE. However, note that the V record (which meets the condition V.PICSIZE >= 500000) is itself a valid candidate for W because it is a row in PIC for that user (satisfying X.USRUID = W.PICUID). Therefore, any user returned by Q2 already has a V record that guarantees the existence of a matching row for W. Thus, the extra join in Q1 does not change the set of users returned, and the queries are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Both queries aim to return the part numbers from PARTS for which the QOH equals the number of SUPPLY entries (with SHIPDATE < 10) for that same part. In Q1 the tuple (PNUM,QOH) is compared to the set of (PNUM, count) computed per part (assuming an implicit GROUP BY on Y.PNUM), while Q2 explicitly joins PARTS with an aggregated subquery (grouped by Y.PNUM) using the conditions X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM and X.QOH = TEMP.CT. They therefore implement the same logic.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 returns only those employees whose (EMP, DEPT) pair appears as (MGR, DEPT) in the DEPT table for departments located at 3, while Q2 returns all employees with no filtering. Therefore, they are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Consider an EMP table with two employees where only one employee matches a DEPT row with LOC=3. In this case, Q1 returns only the matching employee, but Q2 returns both.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 returns the distinct X.X values from A that have a corresponding match in B (X.YA = Y.YB), while Q2, by joining A to itself (via X.X = Y.X) and then to B (X.YA = Z.YB), may produce duplicate output rows when there are multiple rows in A with the same X value. Thus, even though both queries check that an A row has a matching B row, Q2’s extra self-join can multiply rows, causing the results (as a multiset) to differ.
counterexample_dsp: Insert duplicate rows in A with the same X value and a matching B row. For example, if A contains two identical rows (1, 100) and B contains one row (100), Q1 returns one row with value 1 (because it uses DISTINCT) but Q2 returns multiple rows with value 1 due to the self join over A.

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: Q1 filters rows where YX exactly equals 'HELLO' while Q2 filters for the value 'HELLO HI'. They target different data values, so the logic is not equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 100, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 100, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row with YX = 'HELLO' and another with YX = 'HELLO HI'. Then, Q1 will return the row with 'HELLO' and Q2 will return the row with 'HELLO HI'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Both queries restrict R1 to rows where X=1 and require that there exists a row in R2 with the same Y value. In Q2 the extra join with R1 (aliased as Y) only enforces that for any row from R1 (alias X) there exists a row in R1 with the same X value – which is always true (each row self-joins). Thus, both queries return the same result.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Both queries select rows from R where all three columns are equal. In Q1 the condition is A1=A2 and A2=A3, which by transitivity implies A1=A3. Q2 directly uses A1=A2 and A1=A3. Hence, they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries aim to return the distinct set of rows from table R. Q1 does a cross join between R as X and R as Y, which, when SELECT DISTINCT X.* is applied, yields the distinct rows from R. Q2 simply selects the distinct rows from R directly. Since for any nonempty R, the join in Q1 will always pair each X row with at least one Y row (and if R is empty, both queries return no rows), the two queries are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a self-join on R using the condition X.A = Y.A, which filters out rows where A is NULL (because comparing NULLs yields UNKNOWN), while Q2 simply returns the distinct values of A, including NULLs if present. Thus, they are not equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A test database with one row where A is NULL. Q1 returns an empty set because NULL will not match NULL, whereas Q2 returns a set containing NULL.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 return the set of distinct rows (A1, A2) from table R. Q1 uses a self-join on R that, via the equality condition (X.A1 = Y.A1 and X.A2 = Y.A2), guarantees that every row in R has a matching pair with itself, thereby reproducing exactly the distinct rows in R, as Q2 does.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Both queries perform a grouping on R.A and compute the sum of (A+B) for each group. The only difference is the alias (X vs Y), which does not affect the semantics.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries ultimately return the rows from R where X > 50 and X < 200. Although the conditions are applied in a different order (inner vs. outer query), the overall effect is the same.

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries return rows from table R with X values greater than 50 and less than 200. In Q2, the condition X > 50 is applied in a subquery and then further filtered with X < 200 in the outer query, making it semantically equivalent to Q1.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 counts all rows in R while Q2 counts only rows where B is not null. Thus, if any row has B as null, the counts differ.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A table R with one row where B is NULL. Q1 returns 1 because it counts the row, but Q2 returns 0 because it excludes null B values.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries aim to return all distinct rows from table R. In Q1, the WHERE clause uses (X > 50 OR X < 200) which is always true for any non‐NULL integer value (since any integer is either < 200 or > 50). In Q2, the two SELECTs union all rows that satisfy X > 50 and X < 200 respectively; any row that qualifies will appear in at least one of these queries, and duplicates (when a row qualifies both conditions) are eliminated by DISTINCT. Thus, both queries return the same set of rows.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10
q2: SELECT T2.DNAME, T2.CNT AS C FROM (SELECT DEPT0.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM DEPT AS DEPT0 GROUP BY DEPT0.NAME) AS T2 WHERE T2.DNAME = 10
schema: CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPTNO INT, NAME INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 group the DEPT table by NAME to count the rows per department and then filter to only include groups where NAME equals 10. Although Q1 uses a HAVING clause directly on the grouped column and Q2 filters the aggregated subquery using a WHERE clause, they yield the same result under the given schema.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0) Y WHERE Y.X > 0
q2: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries filter table R for rows where X > 0. Q1 wraps the same filtering condition in a subquery and then applies the same condition again, which does not alter the result.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X WHERE X.C IN (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y)
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (C INT);
explanation: Q1 uses a subquery that returns all C values in A and then filters rows such that X.C is in that list. However, due to SQL’s three‐valued logic, if X.C is NULL the comparison (NULL IN (...)) does not evaluate to TRUE, hence such rows are excluded. Q2 simply returns all rows without any filtering. Therefore, rows with a NULL value for C are returned by Q2 but not by Q1.
counterexample: INSERT INTO A VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row with a NULL value for C. Q1 will return no row for the NULL value while Q2 returns the row.

q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B X, A Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (A1 INT, A2 INT);
CREATE TABLE B (B1 INT, B2 INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 join table A and table B on the condition that A.A1 equals B.B1 (even though the table aliases and order are swapped). They return the same set of columns – the columns from A (A1 and A2) and from B (B1 and B2) – with corresponding aliases. Hence, they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM R3) Y
explanation: Q1 takes all rows from R1 and does a cross join with the combined set of rows from R2 and R3 (using UNION ALL), while Q2 explicitly performs two separate cross joins (R1×R2 and R1×R3) and unions their results using UNION ALL. Under the given schema (where R2 and R3 have identical structure), they produce the same result.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB, Y.B AS YB FROM R1 X, R2 Y
q2: SELECT X1.XB AS XB, Y1.YB AS YB FROM (SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R1 X) X1, (SELECT Y.B AS YB FROM R2 Y) Y1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (A INT, B INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Both queries produce the Cartesian product of the B column from R1 and R2. Q2 uses subqueries to project the B column from each table, but it doesn't change the result set compared to Q1.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R UNION ALL SELECT * FROM S) X
schema:
CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
CREATE TABLE S (X INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 produce the exact same set of rows by performing a UNION ALL on the rows from tables R and S. They have the same high-level objective and logic, and thus they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X, (SELECT * FROM B Y WHERE Y.X < 100) Z WHERE X.X = Z.X
q2: SELECT * FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.X = Y.X AND Y.X < 100
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
CREATE TABLE B (X INT);
explanation: Both queries join table A with table B records where B.X < 100, using the join condition A.X = B.X. In Q1 the filtering is done in a subquery while in Q2 it's done directly in the WHERE clause, but the effect is identical, so the queries are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT X.A AS A FROM X X, Y Y WHERE X.K = Y.K
q2: SELECT X1.A AS X1A FROM (SELECT X.A AS A, X.K AS K FROM X X) X1, Y Y WHERE X1.K = Y.K
schema:
CREATE TABLE X (A INT, K INT);
CREATE TABLE Y (A INT, K INT);
explanation: Both queries perform an inner join between tables X and Y using the condition X.K = Y.K and then project the A column from X. Q2 simply wraps X in a subquery which does not change the outcome. Thus, they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0) Z
q2: SELECT * FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both select a cross join of R1 and R2 rows that satisfy the condition Y.X > 0. Q1 applies the condition inside a derived table (filtering R2 before joining), and Q2 applies the same condition in the WHERE clause after the join. Both produce the same result.

q1: SELECT X.A + X.B, X.A/X.B AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT Y.A + Y.B, Y.A/Y.B AS A FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 perform the same operations on table R: they compute the sum of A and B and the ratio A/B using a different table alias. The only difference is the alias names (X versus Y), which does not impact the result. Thus, they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X UNION ALL SELECT * FROM A X WHERE FALSE
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
explanation: Both queries return all rows from table A. The second SELECT in Q1 always yields no rows due to WHERE FALSE, making Q1 equivalent to Q2.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 8
explanation: The two queries only differ in the HAVING condition on COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS): Q1 requires the count to be >5 while Q2 requires it to be >8. Thus, if a department has a sum of credits >10 and a distinct credit count between 6 and 8, Q1 will return it while Q2 will not.
counterexample_dsp: A department with 7 courses having distinct credits (e.g., 1,2,3,4,5,6,7) yields a sum of 28 (which is >10) and distinct count of 7 (which is >5, satisfying Q1, but not >8, so Q2 fails).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME

In Q1, the table of max times (grouped by ORIGIN_CITY) is joined to FLIGHTS so that only flights matching the maximum are returned, and DISTINCT is applied to remove duplicates. In Q2, after joining the subquery (yielding max time per ORIGIN_CITY) with FLIGHTS (using the same equality condition), the query groups by ORIGIN_CITY and DEST_CITY and returns the MAX(ACTUAL_TIME), which is identical to the maximum per city. In effect, both return the same set of rows, so they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME

explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 aim to return, for each origin city, the flight(s) having the maximum ACTUAL_TIME. Q1 does this by joining the FLIGHTS table with a subquery that picks the maximum ACTUAL_TIME per ORIGIN_CITY. Q2, meanwhile, self-joins FLIGHTS to compute the maximum ACTUAL_TIME (via MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME)) for each flight’s origin, then filters for flights where the ACTUAL_TIME equals that maximum. Despite different formulations and grouping details, both queries semantically yield the same set of rows.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the HAVING clause: Q1 requires that a department has more than 5 courses while Q2 requires more than 8 courses. As a result, a department with, say, 7 courses (meeting the SUM(CREDITS) > 10 condition) would be returned by Q1 but not by Q2.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: The two queries differ in the HAVING clause condition for the sum of salaries. Q1 requires SUM(I.SALARY) > 100 while Q2 requires SUM(I.SALARY) >= 100. This means that when the sum of salaries is exactly 100, Q2 will include that group while Q1 will not.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent. Both queries group data by department and check that the sum of department budgets is greater than 100,000. However, Q1’s HAVING clause uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) which counts every occurrence (including duplicates) of the budget value from each join row, while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) which only counts unique budget values. In a scenario where the same department budget value is repeated many times (due to multiple TEACHES rows for a single course), Q1 can have a count greater than 10 while Q2’s distinct count remains 1.

q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in the second HAVING condition. Q1 requires that the group have exactly 4 distinct instructor salaries, while Q2 requires more than 4 distinct salaries. Thus, any department group with exactly 4 distinct instructor salaries (and an average salary > 50000) will appear in Q1 but not in Q2.

The average salary is 75000 (>50000) and the count of distinct salaries is 4. Q1 will return this group; Q2 will not because it requires more than 4 distinct salaries.

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2

explanation: Both queries join the same tables and group by T.SEMESTER with a condition on AVG(C.CREDITS) > 2. explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 join the tables using NATURAL JOIN, which forces the joined DEPT_NAME to be the same in all tuples for a given student (ID). In Q1 the grouping is done on (ID, DEPT_NAME) while in Q2 it is done on ID alone. explanation: Both queries compute the same filtering condition (the course credits equal the maximum level in CS courses from departments with more than two CS courses). q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Both queries join STUDENT with a subquery that aggregates over TAKES JOIN SECTION, but they differ in the subquery’s HAVING clause. Q1 requires that the number of rows in each (ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR) group is greater than 1 (i.e. COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>1), so only groups with at least two rows are retained. (Note that both queries include an outer HAVING clause on COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) that—given the grouping by student—will usually filter out every individual student; however, since that clause is identical in both queries, the essential difference comes from the inner subquery logic.)
counterexample_dsp: Create test data for one student (say, student 1) with exactly one TAKES record linked to a SECTION having TIME_SLOT_ID=2. In this case, the inner subquery of Q2 returns a row (since 2>1 via SUM), whereas Q1’s subquery does not (since COUNT would be 1, not >1). (Also include two other students that have two matching rows so that the outer join is not completely empty even if the outer HAVING is unusual.)

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 groups by both YEAR and COURSE_ID so that it only outputs a row for a (YEAR, COURSE_ID) pair if that course has more than 4 instructors (i.e. COUNT(ID)>4). In contrast, Q2 groups by YEAR only so that even if no single course has more than 4 instructors, the entire year’s joined rows might sum to more than 4 and be returned. In other words, Q1 applies the count condition per course while Q2 applies it per year, which can lead to different results.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a single year (e.g., 2020) with two courses. For course 101 there are 5 teaching records (thus meeting COUNT(ID)>4) and for course 102 there are only 3 teaching records. In Q1, only course 101 yields a row (thus inner query returns one row with T=2020), while Q2 aggregates all rows for 2020 (5+3 = 8) and returns a row because 8>4. Hence Q1 would return 2020 (once) while Q2 returns 2020 (once) but note the inner aggregation is different – if further processing were done (for example summing T over multiple courses), the two queries would behave differently. One can also imagine a situation where no single course qualifies but the total per year does, causing Q2 to return a result when Q1 returns none.

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns all rows from the COURSE table, while Q2 filters the rows and returns only those courses where CREDITS > 3. Thus, they are not equivalent.
counterexample:

INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 102, 1, 4);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two courses: one having CREDITS = 3 and another with CREDITS = 4. Q1 returns both courses, but Q2 returns only the course with CREDITS = 4.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. Q1 returns rows where the course_id in COURSE exactly matches the course_id in TEACHES (for year 2010). Q2, however, returns rows where the course_id in COURSE is greater than or equal to the course_id in TEACHES (for year 2010), which can include additional mismatched pairs.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one COURSE row with COURSE_ID = 2 and two TEACHES rows: one with COURSE_ID = 2 (matching Q1) and one with COURSE_ID = 1. Q1 returns only the matching pair (2, ...), whereas Q2 returns both rows because 2 >= 1 is true, thus producing different results.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation: Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN with the condition INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID, which returns every instructor (with NULLs for TEACHES when there is no matching row) and may join an instructor with any TEACHES row where the instructor's ID is greater than the TEACHES.ID. Q2, on the other hand, is an inner join that returns only those rows where INSTRUCTOR.ID equals TEACHES.ID. The logic is significantly different.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two instructors (with IDs 1 and 2) and one teaches row with ID 1. Q1 will return the instructor with ID 2 joined to the teaches row (because 2 > 1) plus the instructor with ID 1 with a NULL TEACHES (since 1 > 1 is false), while Q2 will only return the instructor with ID 1 joined to the teaches row (because 1 = 1).

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent. Both queries are intended to return the IDs and names of students that, in some year, have taken courses in many distinct time slots. However, Q1 uses the condition COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 4 while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 5. Thus, a student who in a given year has exactly 5 distinct time slots will satisfy Q1’s condition (since 5 > 4) but will fail Q2’s (since 5 is not > 5).
counterexample_dsp: A student (Alice) takes exactly 5 different courses (each in a different time slot) in the same year. In this test data, Q1 returns Alice while Q2 returns no rows.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 selects departments offering a course whose credits equal the global maximum credits found across all courses. In contrast, Q2 compares each course’s credits to the maximum credits within some department (computed per department), and because there’s no join condition linking the course to its own department, a course can match a maximum from any department. This can cause Q2 to return departments that do not offer the course with the global maximum credits.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a COURSE table with three departments: Dept 1 offers only a course with 3 credits; Dept 2 offers a course with 4 credits (global maximum) and another with 2 credits; Dept 3 offers a course with 3 credits. Q1 returns only Dept 2 (since 4 is the global maximum) while Q2 returns all three departments (because courses with 3 credits in Dept 1 and Dept 3 match the per-department max of 3 from another department).
